analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to rebate Medicare when their drug prices rise faster than inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have forced Medicare Part B drug price rebates above inflation, never received a committee vote and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require makers of single-source drugs — brand-name drugs with no competition — to pay a rebate to Medicare whenever their price rises faster than general inflation, measured from early 2016. Part B covers drugs given in doctors' offices, like many cancer and rheumatoid arthritis treatments, where patients pay 20% of the cost out of pocket. The bill sends rebates into the Medicare trust fund and also reduces beneficiaries' coinsurance to reflect the rebates. It never got a hearing or a vote in either committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use Part B drugs, whose 20% coinsurance bills would be adjusted down to reflect the rebates, and taxpayers, because rebates flow into the Medicare trust fund and slow the growth of program spending.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers of single-source drugs must pay Medicare a rebate equal to the amount by which their average sales price exceeds an inflation-adjusted benchmark, per unit sold.
For rebated drugs, the Secretary must pay beneficiaries their coinsurance as if the drug's payment amount had been reduced to reflect the rebate, so patients' out-of-pocket costs drop directly.
Rebate payments are deposited into the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, reducing pressure on Medicare finances and on general-revenue taxpayer subsidies to the program.

The bill gives the Secretary civil monetary penalty authority (up to 2% of a drug's Part B expenditures per quarter) against manufacturers that refuse to pay, and lets MedPAC review manufacturer price reporting.
The Secretary must study extending the same rebate to multisource drugs and to drugs covered by Medicare Advantage plans, opening the door to broader coverage of the policy.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of brand-name, single-source Part B drugs whose prices have risen faster than inflation since early 2016; the faster their prices rise, the larger the rebate.

drawbacks.text: The rebate benchmark is each drug's own price in early 2016 (or shortly after launch for newer drugs), not a comparison to competing drugs, so a manufacturer can avoid the rebate by launching new drugs at very high starting prices and the bill does nothing about initial launch prices at all.

The bill carves out significant categories: drugs paid as part of a bundled hospital outpatient or group payment, drugs included in the dialysis bundled payment, drugs with less than $100 in average annual charges per user, and vaccines are all exempt from the rebate.
The Secretary can reduce or waive the rebate in shortage or other 'exigent circumstances,' a discretion manufacturers could press in disputes over whether price hikes were supply-driven.

Applying the rebate only to single-source drugs leaves multisource drugs outside the system unless the Secretary acts after a three-year study, and the multisource extension is permissive, not mandatory.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it strikes directly at documented above-inflation price increases on drugs with no competition, and it uniquely passes part of the rebate back to patients through lower coinsurance rather than keeping it all in the program. The main weakness is that it does not touch launch prices, so manufacturers can shift pricing behavior to the front end rather than the back end, and its carve-outs leave some expensive categories untouched. On balance it is a modest but well-designed down payment on drug price control, not a comprehensive solution.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, and neither committee ever held a markup or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sander Levin introduced the bill on March 1, 2018.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced.
In the following week it was referred to the Health Subcommittee in each committee, where no further action was taken.
The bill attracted 4 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: they kept charging Medicare prices that rise faster than inflation with no rebate requirement, and Medicare patients and taxpayers received none of the savings the bill would have produced.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 4 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled House committees never advanced the bill to a vote.

industries.note: The bill makes manufacturers pay back to Medicare every dollar their Part B drug prices rise above inflation since early 2016, per unit sold. Their interest in avoiding the rebate runs directly against patients, who pay 20% coinsurance on those inflated prices and would see it lowered under the bill.
The bill authorizes surveys of wholesalers to verify reported prices, with civil penalties up to $100,000 for refusing or falsifying information, but does not otherwise change their economics.
Drugs paid under Medicare Advantage plans are excluded from the rebate for now, but the bill directs a study of including them, so plans face potential future scope expansion.
